prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, in which magic-wavelength trapping of many atoms made timekeeping at the 10^-18 level possible

statement.case_for: I keep my round-1 configuration: a single prize part for B013, Katori and Ye. After the full exchange my reasons are sharper. The chair's first question is whether the clock is a distinct achievement beyond the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 prize for controlling single quantum systems. I think it is, and the citation should say why. The comb gave a ruler for optical frequencies, and the 2012 work controlled one ion at a time. Katori's magic-wavelength lattice trapped thousands of neutral atoms with the light shift cancelled, so statistical precision could be combined with systematic control. That is a different physical scheme and it is what brought stability and accuracy to 1e-18. This was confirmed by independent laboratories on different species, and the clocks are now compared routinely. I weigh that kind of quantitative, independently checked evidence above everything else, as I do when different DFT codes are made to agree. The consequences are also physical: gravitational redshift over millimetres, bounds on drifting constants and dark-matter couplings, and the road to a new SI second. On attribution, Lindroth and Kroll, who know the field, say the two decisive steps are Katori's proposal and early demonstration and Ye's record realisation, with the other groups' contributions real but secondary. I accept that and have no independent way to check it. The pairing follows the citation's own wording, invention and realisation. That also answers Olsson's concern, because the citation rewards the original invention and its decisive realisation and does not simply reward the better-performing second group. On the pending redefinition, I would not wait for it. The scientific evidence is already there, and waiting would make the prize depend on a decision by metrology bodies that is not a physics criterion.
statement.case_against: The reservation I take most seriously is the one all eight of us listed. Metrology has been honoured repeatedly, Ye shared the 2005 prize, and lattice clocks may be read as a very successful continuation instead of a new discovery. It is also a technique and not a new state of matter, which is where my own taste lies. I treat that as a fact about my taste, not as an argument against the work. Omitting Lemonde, Ludlow, Oates, Takamoto, Derevianko and the SYRTE, PTB and NIST groups is a real cost, and I cannot check early priority dates myself. If the committee finds that Katori's invention and Ye's realisation cannot be separated from the others' work well enough for a two-name credit, I would reopen the question. For now the evidence I have heard says they can.

responses.point: Olsson asks that the prize reward the original work and not a second group that did it better, and wants the citation to show that Katori's invention, not Ye's refinement, is what is credited. She also keeps B015 and the Higgs as alternatives and says her own field makes her an interested party on B015.
responses.response: I take this seriously and have written the citation to answer it. It names the invention and the realisation, so the two credits are separate and each can be defended. Katori supplied the magic-wavelength concept and the first strontium lattice clock. Ye took the same scheme to record accuracy and made it a many-body clock. I would not describe Ye's part as mere refinement, because the 1e-18 result is what turned a proposal into an instrument. I agree with your own flag on B015. I still list it as my second alternative because its atomic-resolution and EELS results are what my theory is tested against and are well reproduced. Given your stated interest in electron microscopy, I would give your statements on B015 less weight than your general criterion, and I would expect you to recuse yourself from any vote on it.

responses.point: Kroll replied to me that the clock performance is reproduced at 1e-18 by independent groups and is more mature than B046. He would not oppose B046 on science if the committee wanted a condensed-matter prize, but asks for a later year. He also asks whether a redefinition of the second should be awaited.
responses.response: That is the information I needed from an atomic physicist, and it moves me. I accept that B046 needs more time, and I now treat it as an alternative only. The mechanism of the superconductivity is not settled, and the experimental credit among Cao, Jarillo-Herrero, Dean and Efetov is unresolved. Both are real obstacles to a three-name credit. On the redefinition of the second, I disagree with waiting. The case rests on measured uncertainties and comparisons that already exist. If the redefinition happens first, the citation would be no weaker, so waiting gains nothing in evidence. I also keep my earlier request that the citation stress many-atom stability and relativistic tests, so it does not read as a repeat of 2005 and 2012.

responses.point: Pearce, as chair, observes that broad support may reflect clear attribution as much as scientific weight, and that the Higgs discovery arguably has greater weight but a structurally hard attribution. He keeps B001 and B059 as fallbacks if the Ye precedent is judged disqualifying.
responses.response: I agree that counting support is not a scientific argument, and I have tried to argue from the physics. I do not accept that the Ye precedent is disqualifying. The 2005 prize was for the frequency comb and Hall's and Hänsch's contribution to optical spectroscopy. The lattice clock is a different invention, and Ye's role in it is separate. On the Higgs, I accept that the physics is unquestioned and that I am outside my field. Because of that I cannot offer an attribution among Gianotti, Della Negra, Jenni and Virdee that I would defend, and I picked three names only as a placeholder at opening. In my view the attribution problem has no scientific answer inside the three-person limit, so B001 is better held for a year when a defensible attribution exists. I would not let that block B013.

responses.point: Mehlig says maturity is the difference between B046 and B013: the single-particle flat bands are established, but the superconductivity is not settled and credit among Bistritzer-MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero, Cao, Dean, Efetov and earlier theory is unresolved. Waiting a few years carries little risk. He also keeps KPZ only as an alternative.
responses.response: I accept his point on maturity and drop my round-1 line that widespread reproduction of the phenomena is enough. Reproducing correlated insulators and superconductivity is not the same as understanding them, and the credit question is where a three-name set would break down. I do not agree that it should wait indefinitely. Reproduction of the discovery is already strong, and I hope the committee returns to it in a few years. As to KPZ, I appreciate his candour that it has almost no support here. Parisi's earlier prize and the exact-solution contributors outside the credited names make a clean three-name credit hard, so I see no basis to put it ahead of B013 this year.

uncertainties: Whether the committee is satisfied that the lattice clock is distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes. I think it is, but members outside atomic physics may weigh the precedent more heavily.
Whether Katori and Ye can be separated from Lemonde, Ludlow, Oates, Takamoto and others as firmly as Lindroth and Kroll say. I rely on their recollection of priority dates and have not checked them.
How the citation should be worded to credit invention and realisation while remaining fair to other groups.
Whether B046 will have a settled mechanism and clearer experimental credit in a few years. I see the case as strong but not ready for a three-name credit.
Whether a second prize part is justified. No member has proposed a pairing partner with clean attribution, and I do not want to add one for balance.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict with Katori, Ye or any lattice-clock group. My Uppsala theory work is computational and linked to electron spectroscopy and 2D materials, with no personal or institutional tie to any credited person on the shortlist. I note this for B015 and B046, which I list as alternatives, because they are close to my own research interests. I am outside my field on B013 and rely on colleagues in atomic physics for priority questions. I support Olsson's recusal on B015 and Johansson's on B054.
